mstts:express-as.prosody: As we wrap up our journey together, just take a moment. If you’ve made it this far, you’ve really walked side by side with the mortician—through those quiet halls, hearing the questions that linger in every heart, and discovering the unexpected beauty that can show up, even in life’s hardest moments. Death might seem strange, maybe even a little unsettling, but it’s not the enemy. If anything, it’s a teacher—reminding us what it truly means to be alive. So, what can you carry forward from this? First, asking honest questions about death is perfectly natural. In fact, those questions deserve answers that are thoughtful and kind. And when it comes to decomposition, it’s really just a process of transformation—not something to be scared of, or to shy away from. Rituals, whether they’re traditional or something uniquely your own, give us a way to honor and remember the people we love. And grief—it’s unpredictable, but you’ll find that sharing it with others makes it just a little easier to bear. Facing our own mortality isn’t just about endings. It can actually inspire us to live bigger, and to love more deeply. Here’s something to remember: you don’t need to have all the answers. It’s enough to stay curious, to ask, and to listen. If you ever feel afraid or unsure, you’re not alone. Every single person wonders about these things at some point. The mortician’s greatest gift wasn’t her technical skills—it was her willingness to meet every question with patience and a gentle heart. So, let yourself be curious. Don’t be afraid to talk about what scares you. Create rituals that feel true to your heart. And when it’s time to say goodbye, trust that love lasts, even as life changes shape. In the end, the cycle of life and death isn’t something to conquer—it’s something to honor. When you face it with open eyes and an open heart, you might just find that the unknown isn’t so scary after all. And in meeting it bravely, you give yourself the chance to be more fully, beautifully alive.
